Psalm 23
sahm TWEN-tee-three
scripture portion
From the superscription “A Psalm of David”; the twenty-third in the Psalter, known from its first words as “The LORD is my shepherd.”

Biblical Definition

Psalm 23 is the best loved of all the psalms, a song of David in which the shepherd-king confesses the LORD to be his own Shepherd. In six brief verses it unfolds the whole care of God over His people. The Shepherd supplies every need, so that the believer shall not want; He leads to green pastures and still waters and restores the soul; He guides in the paths of righteousness for His name’s sake. Even in the valley of the shadow of death the sheep fears no evil, for the Shepherd is present, and His rod and staff comfort. The figure then changes to a host who spreads a table in the presence of enemies, anoints the head with oil, and fills the cup to overflowing. The psalm closes in settled assurance: goodness and mercy shall follow all the days of life, and the believer shall dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. The Lord Jesus takes up this very image when He calls Himself the Good Shepherd who gives His life for the sheep. The dictionary receives the psalm not as a sentimental comfort merely, but as a confession of the sovereign, particular, persevering care of God for every one of His own, from the green pasture of this life to the everlasting house of the next.

Webster 1828 Definition

David’s beloved psalm confessing the LORD as Shepherd, who supplies, restores, guides, and comforts His people through death itself to the house of the LORD for ever.

expand to see more

PSALM 23, the psalm of David beginning “The LORD is my shepherd.”

Confesses the LORD as Shepherd who supplies every need, so the believer shall not want.

Leads to green pastures and still waters and restores the soul.

Gives no fear in the valley of the shadow of death, for the Shepherd is present.

Closes in the assurance of dwelling in the house of the LORD for ever.

Key Scripture

Psa 23:1 — "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."

Psa 23:4 — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

Psa 23:6 — "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."

Joh 10:11 — "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."

Modern Corruption

The psalm is sentimentalized into a vague comfort, severed from the sovereign Shepherd and the particular care it confesses.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the comfort of Psalm 23 rests wholly on the character and sovereignty of the Shepherd. “I shall not want” is not a promise of ease but of sufficiency: the sheep lacks nothing because the Shepherd supplies all. Modern sentiment reduces the psalm to a soothing poem read at funerals; the believer must recover it as a bold confession of the particular, persevering care of God over each of His own.

Where a corruption presses, it is the detaching of the psalm from Christ. The Lord Jesus claims the very image: “I am the good shepherd.” The valley of the shadow of death holds no terror because the Shepherd Himself passed through death for the sheep and rose again. To read the psalm without Him is to keep the comfort while losing its ground; the rod and staff that comfort are held by nail-pierced hands.

Hebrew Roots

The psalm draws on the shepherd imagery deep in Israel’s life, fulfilled in Christ the Good Shepherd.

expand to see more

Hebrew rō’eh — a shepherd, one who tends and feeds the flock.

Hebrew nāḥam and kindred terms — to comfort, console, the comfort of rod and staff.

The “valley of the shadow of death,” Hebrew tsalmaveth, deep darkness.

The shepherd figure runs from Abel and the patriarchs to David to Christ.

Greek poimēn — shepherd, the title Jesus claims in John 10.

Usage

"Psalm 23 is read at deathbeds and funerals for its assurance through the valley of death."

"It is preached as the confession of God’s particular, persevering care for each believer."

"Its shepherd imagery is connected with Christ’s claim to be the Good Shepherd."
